#<center>**Minor Child-Centered Estate Plan{[if IsGeauxMarriedTF]} for a Married Couple{[endif]}**</center>

The Minor Child-Centered Estate Plan is well suited for families with young children.  The plan includes the following:

**Last Will and Testament**: This document provides for {[if IsGeauxMarriedTF]}a bequest to your spouse (either outright or in usufruct) and, if you are not survived by your spouse, {[endif]}bequests to your children (or other persons you select) in whatever proportions you choose.  The Will includes a special provision to nominate a tutor (a/k/a “guardian”) for your minor child(ren), which is the person to act as a surrogate parent for your minor child if you are no longer with us.  The Last Will and Testament also includes a Trust for your children that will prevent your child from owning assets at too young an age.  

This estate planning package also includes a **Financial Power of Attorney**, a **Medical Power of Attorney**, and an **Advanced Healthcare Directive** (a/k/a “Living Will”).

{[if IsGeauxAppTF && IsGeauxMarriedTF]}
The plan includes reciprocal documents for your spouse.

{[endif]}
All bequests to your children (or other persons you select) can either be in trust or outright.

#<center>**Power of Attorney Supplement {[if IsGeauxMarriedTF]}for Two People{[else]}for One Person{[endif]}**</center>

The Power of Attorney Supplement to your estate plan is well suited for families with a young adult child or student who is over the age of eighteen (18), or families with an agent parent, or any other person who needs to authorize someone to act for them legally. The Power of Attorney Supplement includes a **Financial Power of Attorney**, a **Medical Power of Attorney**, and an **Advanced Healthcare Directive** (a/k/a “Living Will”) for one person. These documents would authorize someone to make legal or financial decisions for your adult child, aging parent, or any other person, as well as access protected health information, consent to medical procedures, or make care arrangements if they are unable to do so.

#
**Trust-Based Estate Plan{[if IsGeauxMarriedTF]} for a Married Couple{[endif]}**
The Trust-Based Estate Plan includes a **Revocable Living Trust**, a **Pourover Last Will and Testament**, a **Financial Power of Attorney**, and a **Medical Power of Attorney**, as well as an **Advanced Healthcare Directive** (a/k/a “Living Will”) for you{[if GeauxSpouseYesTrustTF]} and your spouse{[endif]}. The Trust-Based Estate Plan also includes an **Act of Donation** for your principal residence. The person creating a Revocable Living Trust is referred to as the “Settlor”, which would be you{[if GeauxSpouseYesTrustTF]} and or your Spouse{[endif]}. You {[if GeauxSpouseYesTrustTF]}and your Spouse {[endif]}will be appointed as the initial Trustee{[if GeauxSpouseYesTrustTF]}s{[endif]} of your trust. The Trustee is essentially in charge of managing assets and making distributions. You {[if GeauxSpouseYesTrustTF]}and your Spouse {[endif]} will also be named as Beneficiary of the trust for life. Beneficiaries are the person(s) entitled to received distributions from trust. {[if IsGeauxMarriedTF]} Distributions to the Surviving Spouse (i.e., whichever of you lives longest) will continue to be held in in trust for life. Following the death of a Spouse, the Surviving Spouse will be the sole Trustee and Beneficiary of the trust for their lifetime. {[endif]} Once you have {[if IsGeauxMarriedTF]}both {[endif]}passed away, distributions to your children or other beneficiaries you name are outright. The process of transferring assets to trust is referred to as “trust funding.” Your trust must be properly funded to avoid probate. The **Act of Donation of Principal Residence** included with your plan effects a donation of your principal residence to trust with a reserved lifetime usufruct which allows you and your spouse to use the residence for the rest of your days before full ownership is vested in the trust. You will need to obtain and input the legal description for your principal residence. Your home will continue to qualify for the homestead tax exemption, but understand you must contact your parish tax assessor to determine whether you need to refile for the homestead exemption. You must also record the Act of Donation of principal residence in the Conveyance Records of the Parish District Court in which your residence is located. Please note that in order to avoid probate, all assets that you own must be transferred to your revocable living trust (other than assets governed by beneficiary designation, like life insurance, annuities, or retirement plans, or usufruct property if you are the usufructuary). Retirement plan and other qualified plans should not be transferred to your trust to avoid disqualification of the plan resulting in income tax and penalties. Please also note that you must contact your homeowners insurer, as well as any other property and casualty insurer to request that your revocable living trust be named as an additional insured of any property owned by the trust. We do not recommend transferring vehicles to your revocable living trust because an affidavit procedure exists to transfer vehicles outside of probate in Louisiana. However, if you do so, be sure to contact your auto-insurer to have your revocable living trust named as an additional insured under your automobile insurance policy.

{[if ESignTF]}<accent red> WARNING: Certain transactions (e.g., conveying real estate) require an "Authentic Act" before a notary and two witnesses for validity in Louisiana. Use caution when executing a Power of Attorney by electronic signature as such powers may not be properly conveyed to a designated Agent.</accent>{[endif]}

##
Any Other People or Entities{[if GeauxPoATF]} Who Will Serve as Agents{[endif]}

A Last Will and Testament is essentially a gift that takes place at death. It can be changed at any time prior to death as long as the maker has capacity. A Will directs how debts of a person are to be paid at death, who will receive assets, who will control administration of an estate, and appoints tutors (a/k/a guardian) of minor children. This Will is intended to be a basic document which has certain limitations, including: 1. All bequests to your spouse (if you are married) are outright free of trust or in usufruct. This Will does not include a testamentary trust for a spouse. 2. If you are unmarried, or your spouse predeceases you, then all bequests to your child(ren) (or anyone else you select) are either outright or in trust until they reach an age you deem old enough to receive assets directly. If you have any questions, please contact us HERE or at 1 (855) 213-6300.

####
Pourover Last Will and Testament
A Pourover Last Will and Testament is an ancillary document that should be included with any trust-based plan. A trust must be properly funded to avoid probate. The purpose of a Pourover Will is to convey assets that were not transferred to trust prior to the death of a Settlor. Like a decanter, whatever assets remain outside of trust “pourover” into the trust by way of the Pourover Will. A properly funded trust will not need to utilize the Pourover Will, so the inclusion of this document is just a backstop to ensure the trust remains the centerpiece of a trust-based estate plan. The only variable you need to consider in a Pourover Will is the choice of your Independent Executor, who would be in charge of opening a Louisiana succession to convey omitted assets to your Revocable Living Trust. If you have any questions, please contact us HERE or at 1 (855) 213-6300.

{[Client.NameCO]} can choose to leave {[Client.Gender.HisHer|else: "his or her"]} estate to {[if MarriedTF]}{[Spouse.NameCO]}{[endif]} either outright or in usufruct.

The term “usufruct” is a unique Louisiana concept that refers to the “use” and “fruits” of property: Usa (use) + fruct (fruits). A Louisiana usufruct is basically a right to use any property subject to the usufruct, as well as the right to enjoy the “fruits” of such property, such as interest, rents, royalties, or dividends. A usufruct can be granted for the life of {[if MarriedTF]}{[Spouse.NameCO]}{[endif]}, or it can terminate upon the happening an event such as {[if MarriedTF]}{[Spouse.NameCO]}{[endif]}'s remarriage.  

The usufruct created in {[Client.NameCO]}'s Will includes the “right of disposition” which means {[if MarriedTF]}{[Spouse.NameCO]}{[endif]} can sell property subject to the usufruct without the need to obtain consent or permission from anyone.  The usufruct under {[Client.NameCO]}'s Will is “without bond”, which means that {[if MarriedTF]}{[Spouse.NameCO]}{[endif]} will not have to post security for the value of the usufruct for the benefit of those who will inherit whatever remains of the usufruct property when it terminates.  

The people who inherit property upon termination of the usufruct are referred to as “naked owners” in Louisiana. In {[Client.NameCO]}'s case, the naked owners will be the people who receive {[Client.NameCO]}'s final distributions in the "Final Distributions" section below.

####
Revocable Living Trust
The centerpiece of the Trust-Based Estate Plan is a Revocable Living Trust, which is an agreement for the management and disposition of your property designed to avoid the expense and administrative burden of probate. Once the agreement is signed by you, your assets are then transferred to the trust. The assets are held in trust for your benefit for the rest of your life and, thereafter, distributed to beneficiaries that you choose. Most commonly the person creating a Revocable Living Trust (referred to as the “Settlor”) would name themself as both Trustee and Beneficiary. The Trustee is essentially in charge of managing assets and making distributions. Beneficiaries are the person entitled to received distributions from trust. Children or other persons can also be named as beneficiaries to receive assets upon the last to die of the Settlors (or before in your discretion). Trust assets are distributed outright free of trust to the beneficiaries after you have{[if MarriedTF]} both{[endif]} passed. A Revocable Trust can be amended, modified, or revoked at any time and for any reason as long as you are alive and have mental capacity in case you change your wishes. If you have any questions, please contact us HERE or at 1 (855) 213-6300.

###
Trust {[if EstateAppTF]}Liquidation, First Rights of Refusal, and {[endif]}Specific Bequests

A *specific gift* is a gift of specific personal property (personal items, a certain amount of money, vehicles, a house, land, etc.) that will be given outright to selected people or entities upon  {[if MarriedTF]}either the death of {[Client.NameCO]}, the death of {[Spouse.NameCO]}, or once both {[Client.NameCO]} and {[Spouse.NameCO]} have passed{[else]}{[Client.NameCO]}'s death{[endif]}. 

Any property not specifically given to a person (or entity) will be divided among the people who receive the Trust's final distributions in the "Final Distributions" section below.

<accent red>NOTE: A SORT **will be included by default** regardless of the selection to allow flexibility regarding the beneficiary designation of a retirement plan in the event **nursing home asset protection** becomes a goal.  ALSO NOTE: A restriction on access to principal is required for **nursing home asset protection**, which will accelerate required minimum distributions to a SORT f/b/o the sole benefit of a surviving spouse. **Select Trustees below.**</accent>

<accent red>{[if peek(MaritalTrustType == "MaritalFed")]}**CAUTION: Do not select the "Marital Trust with QTIP / Credit Shelter shares for FET optimization" if this Living Trust is an Irrevocable Asset Protection Trust (APT) because the QTIP share cannot restrict access to the principal.**{[else]}**NOTE: If this is an Irrevocable Asset Protection Trust (APT), the Marital Trust will include a *restriction on access to principal*, which will prevent a QTIP election for Federal Estate Tax purposes.**{[endif]}</accent>

The Surviving Spouse will then become the sole Trustee of the Lifetime Trust. Once the Surviving Spouse passes{[else]}Once you pass{[endif]}, your assets will be distributed outright or in trust to the recipients selected below (usually children or other persons you want to receive your estate), in the percentages selected.

In the event a person receives an interest through the occurrence of an unforeseeable event, such as the death of a named beneficiary, a contingent Under-Age Beneficiary Trust is established if the person is below eighteen (18) years of age to ensure the person receiving the interest is at least the legal age of majority to receive assets. 

For example, if you name a child as a legatee under the Trust and your child predeceases you, leaving behind children (your grandchildren), your grandchildren will receive your predeceased child’s interest by representation under Louisiana law. In this case, your GeauxPlans Revocable Living Trust directs the interest to be held for the benefit of your grandchild until age eighteen (18), at which time the contingent Under-Age Beneficiary Trust will terminate and the assets will be distributed outright to the grandchild.

<accent red>CAUTION: In most instances, we recommend setting the minimum age to remove a Trustee no earlier than the later of: (1) the last age of distribution for any Separate Share Trusts created for any Trust beneficiaries, or (2) the age of distribution for any Under-Stated-Age Beneficiaries.</accent>

{[if IsGeauxAppTF]}Enter information for your Power(s) of Attorney here{[else]}Power(s) of Attorney{[endif]}
***

####<center>A power of attorney allows you to appoint someone you know and trust to make your financial and health care decisions when you cannot.</center>

If you become incapacitated without this legal document, then you and your family will likely be involved in a court proceeding wherein a judge will determine who should make these decisions for you under court supervision!

####
A Financial Power of Attorney (FPOA) is a legal document that allows an individual to designate another person to make financial decisions for him or her when he or she cannot make decisions for himself or herself.
Your agent's powers will include the full power to act and transact business on your behalf, including, but not limited to, purchasing and selling assets, establishing legal entities, such as trusts and limited liability companies, making and accepting donations, participating in legal proceedings, and virtually any other legal act that you could personally undertake. If you have any questions, please contact us HERE or at 1 (855) 213-6300.

####
{[Client.NameCO]}'s Initial Agents for Financial Power of Attorney
Choose {[Client.NameCO]}'s initial Agents for the Financial Power of Attorney (the person {[Client.Gender.HeShe]} wants to make financial decisions for {[Client.Gender.HimHer]} if {[Client.Gender.HeShe]} is incapacitated). {[Client.NameCO]} may select a Co-Agent to serve at the same time as the Initial Agent. Decisions of Co-Agents will be made jointly by mutual consent{[if MarriedTF]}. People usually choose their spouse as their first and sole initial Agent, but that is not required{[endif]}.

####
{[Client.NameCO]}'s Successor Agents for Financial Power of Attorney
The successor agents will serve if all of the initial agents are unable to serve. These successor agents will serve in the order they are entered. Successor agents are not required, but are usually recommended.

####
A Health Care Power of Attorney (HCPOA) is a legal document that allows an individual to designate another person to make medical decisions for him or her when he or she cannot make decisions for himself or herself.
In other words it names someone who stands in your shoes and tells the doctors what to do or what not do for you. A person need not be terminally ill, elderly, or facing high risk activities to execute a HCPOA. Health care decisions include the power to consent, refuse consent or withdraw consent to any type of medical care, treatment, service or procedure. A HCPOA is also referred to as health care proxy, medical power of attorney and Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care. If you have any questions, please contact us HERE or at 1 (855) 213-6300.

{[if IsGeauxAppTF]}Enter information for your Healthcare Directive here{[else]}Healthcare Directive{[endif]}
***

#####
Also known as a “Living Will”
A statement of your wishes regarding the types of medical life support measures you prefer to have, or have withheld if you are in a terminal condition and cannot express your wishes yourself. Without this legal document, your physician will spare no expense to prolong your life. A Healthcare Directive (sometimes referred to as a “Living Will”) is a document that instructs your healthcare provider to withhold life sustaining procedures in the event two (2) physicians certify that you are in a terminal and irreversible condition and that your death will occur whether or not life-sustaining procedures are utilized to artificially prolong your life. If you wish to make this directive, you essentially have two choices: (1) to withhold all life sustaining procedures, including nutrition and hydration; or (2) to withhold all life-sustaining procedures, except nutrition and hydration. You will not be conscious or able to communicate in this end-of-life state, so nutrition connotes a feeding tube and hydration would be administered intravenously. You must initial next to your choice as indicated on the form. If you have any questions, please contact us HERE or at 1 (855) 213-6300.

properties.helpText:
UNDER-STATED-AGE BENEFICIARY TRUST:
This trust generally serves a contingency in the event a younger person acquires a beneficial interest by representation. You also select this contingent trust as a simple solution for younger beneficiaries in lieu of a stand-alone Term Trust for a younger person. The USA trust has only one age of distribution, while a stand-alone Term Trust can be more personalized. 

INCOMPETENT OR DISABLED BENEFICIARY TRUST:
This contingent trust is intended to serve as a standby Special Needs Trust in the event circumstances change. Create a standalone SNT for any beneficiary with known special needs. 

RETIREMENT TRUST:
Select this to include a Retirement Trust f/b/o Beneficiaries other than a Surviving Spouse. Select the Spouse-Only Retirement Trust to direct spousal retirement benefits.

properties.name: APTReservePowerAmendTF
properties.label: Select to reserve the power to amend the trust to add or remove {[if !(peek(PlanType == "StandaloneTrust") && peek(StandaloneTrust == "SNT"))]}**Residual Beneficiaries**{[else]}**Principal Beneficiaries**{[endif]} of the {[if peek(PlanType == "StandaloneTrust") && peek(StandaloneTrust == "SNT")]}**Special Needs Trust**{[else]}**Lifetime Trust**{[endif]}.
properties.helpText:
This provision can be used with an Irrevocable Asset Protection Trust to allow a {[StateLawSelect.GrantorReference]} to retain control of the ultimate disposition of trust assets.

NOTE: A {[StateLawSelect.GrantorReference]} cannot be named as a principal beneficiary despite a reserved power to amend, which would defeat a substantial purpose of an Irrevocable Asset Protection Trust - namely to protect assets placed into trust by the {[StateLawSelect.GrantorReference]}.

properties.name: SNTIncomeTaxStatus
properties.label: Select the desired income tax status of the Trust:
properties.helpText:
GRANTOR TRUST
- The {[StateLawSelect.GrantorReference]} retains enough control over the trust that the IRS treats the grantor as the owner for income tax purposes. 
- Income from the trust is reported on the {[StateLawSelect.GrantorReference]}'s personal tax return. 
- Examples include a revocable living trust or a specific type of irrevocable trust like an IDGT.

NON-GRANTOR TRUST
- The {[StateLawSelect.GrantorReference]} gives up sufficient control and interest in the trust. 
- The trust is considered a separate legal and tax entity, and the trust itself or its beneficiaries are responsible for paying the income tax. 
- Assets are generally excluded from the {[StateLawSelect.GrantorReference]}'S gross estate for estate tax purposes. 

INTENTIONALLY DEFECTIVE GRANTOR TRUST (IDGT)
- A type of irrevocable grantor trust designed for estate planning. 
- The {[StateLawSelect.GrantorReference]} gives up the assets for estate tax purposes, meaning they are not included in the grantor's taxable estate. 
- However, the {[StateLawSelect.GrantorReference]} intentionally retains certain powers that cause the trust to be treated as a "grantor trust" for income tax purposes. 
- This allows the {[StateLawSelect.GrantorReference]} to pay the trust's income taxes from their personal assets, enabling the trust's assets to grow faster and free from income tax. 
- The "defect" is the retained power that makes it a grantor trust for income tax, while the irrevocability and lack of direct control for estate tax purposes make it a strategic estate planning tool.

properties.name: QDOT
properties.label: **QDOT: Select if one or both Spouses are NOT United States citizens**
properties.helpText:
A QDOT (Qualified Domestic Trust) is used to preserve the federal estate tax marital deduction when a U.S. citizen is married to a non-U.S. citizen spouse.

**Why a QDOT is Necessary**

Under federal estate tax law, the unlimited marital deduction is not available for transfers to a non-citizen spouse. Without planning, assets passing outright to a non-citizen spouse may be subject to estate tax at the first death.

**A QDOT allows the estate to:**

- Defer estate tax that would otherwise be due at the first spouse’s death, and

- Treat the transfer as qualifying for the marital deduction so long as the QDOT requirements are met.

**What a QDOT Does**

Holds assets for the benefit of the non-citizen surviving spouse

Allows income distributions to the spouse

Defers estate tax until:

- Principal is distributed (subject to exceptions), or

- The surviving spouse dies

**When a QDOT Is Used**

A QDOT is appropriate when:

- One spouse is not a U.S. citizen, and

- The couple wants to defer estate tax rather than pay it at the first death.
